title: PRIME – Physical Exercise and Its Impact on Inflammation-Driven Processes, Immune Cell Function, Cardiopulmonary Fitness, Muscle Strength and Quality of Life in Patients with Myeloproliferative Neoplasms
summary:
The purpose of this study is to determine whether patients with myelofibrosis benefit from physical activity. In particular, the study will examine quality of life, the impact on the pro-inflammatory environment, and cardiovascular fitness.
As part of this study, we intend to use a structured approach—including quality-of-life questionnaires, blood tests, and sports medicine examinations—to determine whether targeted physical activity leads to positive effects in these areas.
The study is expected to last 3 months for each participant.
As part of one of your scheduled initial consultations with PD Dr. med. Stefanie Jilg in the Department of Hematology and Oncology at Maxvorstadt or with Dr. med. Peter Herhaus at the TUM Klinikum Rechts der Isar, you will also be introduced to our colleagues in sports medicine. They will perform a spiroergometry test, an echocardiogram, a strength test, and a bioimpedance measurement, and will advise you on a suitable exercise program or physical activity based on your current physical condition and “fitness level.”
Specifically, this means:
BIA (Bioimpedance Analysis)
A measurement using special scales or electrodes, in which a weak electrical current flows through the body. This allows for an estimate of the amount of fat, muscle mass, and water in the body. Thus, not only is a person’s weight determined, but also their “body composition.”

Spiroergometry
A test in which a person exercises on a stationary bike or treadmill while oxygen and CO₂ levels in the exhaled air are measured. This tests the capacity of the heart, lungs, and circulatory system under stress.
Echocardiography
An ultrasound examination of the heart to assess cardiac output and the heart valves.
 
Strength Test
This is a simple, standardized test of muscle strength (e.g., using a hand dynamometer, which you squeeze as hard as you can). The goal is to objectively measure muscle strength.

This appointment is part of standard care and can also be scheduled outside of the PRIME program.
If you decide to participate, after receiving detailed information and signing a written informed consent form, you will be assigned a study-specific patient number and given a specific patient diary. In this diary, you should record daily whether and for how long you performed the agreed-upon exercises, as well as your other physical activities.
We will also ask you to note in the diary if you have been on sick leave due to an infection or if you experience a thromboembolic event (thrombosis, stroke, pulmonary embolism, etc.).

After 12 weeks, you will have another follow-up appointment with the sports medicine team to assess your progress and discuss any problems or challenges you may be facing. All data collected during these examinations will be provided to you upon request. There is no cost to you as long as you have statutory or private health insurance.
To measure the effects of physical activity on your quality of life and symptoms such as fatigue, we will ask you to fill out questionnaires for us every 2 weeks (for a total of 7 times). You will need to complete the following forms at home 5 times:
• Short Form 36 Health Survey (SF-36):    36 questions
• MPN-10 questionnaire            10 questions
• BFI (Brief Fatigue Inventory)        13 questions

You are probably already familiar with these questionnaires from our routine clinical practice.
Blood samples will also be drawn at your first appointment as part of your regular clinical follow-up, as well as at 6 weeks and 12 weeks (which often correspond to the standard intervals for follow-up examinations). You have likely heard of most of the laboratory values being tested, as these are routine blood tests for your condition. As part of the study, we can offer you a cytokine panel test free of charge at Week 0 (before starting the recommended physical activity) and at Week 12. These results will also be provided to you upon request and may be familiar to you as IGeL (Individual Health Services) offered by your primary care physician or specialist.
Since the collection of these blood samples is not part of routine clinical practice, we are required to inform you in this letter about the potential risks associated with venous blood collection:
Blood draws from a vein are usually well tolerated and rarely lead to complications. However, the puncture site may experience complications such as bruising, the formation of small scars, hardening, abnormal sensations around the puncture site due to accidental injury to tiny skin nerves, infection, phlebitis, thrombosis, or the dislodging of tiny blood clots. Circulatory reactions may also occur rarely; in very rare cases, an artery may be punctured, leading to significant blood loss. The blood sample is collected as part of routine diagnostic procedures to minimize potential risks.
By giving your consent to participate in the PRIME study, we will record your personal data—including your medical history—in pseudonymized form, consistent with our patient records, and correlate your blood test results with your personal medical history and the extent of your physical activity.
We therefore assume that even very moderate but regular physical activity has a positive impact, particularly on the cardiovascular system, the inflammatory environment (i.e., the disease-related, upregulated inflammatory processes in your body), symptoms such as fatigue (pathological exhaustion), and quality of life.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Inclusion criteria: Inclusion criteria:
• Age > 18 years
• Diagnosis of primary myelofibrosis (PMF) according to the revised WHO criteria, or secondary myelofibrosis following polycythemia vera (PPV-MF) or essential thrombocythemia (PET-MF) according to the IWG-MRT criteria
• Stable for at least 6 months on a JAK inhibitor, defined by consistent dosing, absence of disease progression, and absence of serious adverse effects that would lead to prompt  discontinuation of the medication
Stable (residual) hematopoiesis maintained for over 6 months with   
absolute neutrophil count ≥ 0.5–1.0 × 10⁹/L and
Hb (pre-transfusion) ≥ 6 g/dL and
platelet count ≥ 50 × 10⁹/L and
blood blast percentage ≤ 10%
Exclusion criteria:
Exclusion criteria: • Presence of other serious physical or mental health conditions that could influence the interpretation of study data or increase the patient’s risk
• History of allogeneic stem cell transplantation
• Inability to tolerate physical exercise
